title: Revisiting Maximum 𝑘-Biplex Search Through 𝑘-Bounded-Degree Deletion

paper.title: Revisiting Maximum k k -Biplex Search Through k k -Bounded-Degree Deletion
paper.abstract:
Abstract. Biplex, as a relaxation of the biclique model, has emerged as an important cohesive subgraph model for bipartite graph analysis. The maximum k k -biplex search problem aims to identify the k k -biplex with maximum number of edges and has been widely applied in various real-world applications, including community detection, online recommendation, and fraud detection. However, the problem is NP-hard, and existing exact algorithms remain inefficient on large-scale bipartite graphs with large values of k k (e.g., k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 ).
In this paper, we revisit the maximum k k -biplex search problem from a complementary perspective. We reveal a novel structural duality: finding a maximum k k -biplex in a bipartite graph is equivalent to finding a minimal k k -bounded-degree deletion in its complement graph. Based on this observation, we propose a novel deletion-based algorithm for the maximum k k -biplex search problem. We theoretically prove that the proposed algorithm achieves a worst-case time complexity of O ∗ ​ ( γ k n ) O^{*}(\gamma_{k}^{n}) , where γ k < 2 \gamma_{k}<2 . Specifically, γ 1 = 1.725 \gamma_{1}=1.725 , γ 2 = 1.856 \gamma_{2}=1.856 , and γ 3 = 1.928 \gamma_{3}=1.928 .
To further enhance practical efficiency, we develop several effective upper-bounding techniques and a heuristic strategy for obtaining high-quality initial solutions, which substantially reduce the search space. Extensive experiments on eight real-world bipartite graphs demonstrate the efficiency of our approach, which achieves up to four orders of magnitude speedups over state-of-the-art algorithms.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Bipartite graphs are fundamental data structures for modeling interactions between two distinct groups of entities, such as user-item interactions in e-commerce networks ( Li et al., 2023 ; Yu and Long, 2023 ) , author-publication relationships in academic networks ( Ley, 2002 ) , and gene-protein associations in computational biology networks ( Voggenreiter et al., 2012 ; Eren et al., 2013 ; Xie et al., 2019 ) . Identifying cohesive subgraphs is a core task in bipartite graph mining, since such subgraphs often reveal meaningful groups with strong cross-side associations. For example, in computational biology networks, cohesive subgraphs can capture groups of genes and proteins with strong expression associations, thereby helping identify functional modules or disease-related biological pathways ( Xie et al., 2019 ) . As a classical cohesive subgraph model in bipartite graphs, the biclique has been widely studied and applied in many scenarios ( Braun et al., 2017 ; Lehmann et al., 2008 ; Langston et al., 2008 ) . A biclique is a complete bipartite subgraph, where every vertex on one side is connected to all vertices on the other side. The maximum biclique search problem aims to find a biclique containing the maximum number of edges, which has attracted considerable attention in recent years ( Liu et al., 2006 ; Alzahrani and Horadam, 2019 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Gillis and Glineur, 2014 ; Feng et al., 2018 ; Lyu et al., 2020 ) . However, real-world network data are inevitably affected by observation noise, measurement errors, and missing data ( Li et al., 2008 ; Liu et al., Conference Proceedings ) . Due to the strict complete-connectivity requirement, the biclique is unable to represent cohesive communities that contain a small number of missing edges, which limits its practical application. To address this limitation, the k k -biplex model was introduced as a relaxation of the biclique and has attracted increasing attention in recent years ( Yu et al., 2022 ; Dai et al., 2024 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2021 ; Luo et al., Conference Proceedings ; Yu and Long, 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) . Formally, in a k k -biplex of a bipartite graph, each vertex has at most k k non-neighbors. This relaxation allows limited missing edges while preserving its cohesion, and has been applied to many real-world tasks such as online recommendation ( Gunnemann et al., 2011 ; Poernomo and Gopalkrishnan, 2009 ) , community detection ( Dai et al., 2023 ; Hao et al., 2020 ) , and fraud detection ( Dai et al., 2023 ; Yu and Long, 2023 ) . In this paper, we study the problem of finding a k k -biplex with the maximum number of edges, which is referred to as the maximum k k -biplex search problem. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for any positive integer k k ( Pan et al., 2024 ) , implying that no polynomial-time algorithm exists unless P = NP \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP} . To solve the maximum k k -biplex search problem, several exact algorithms have been developed in recent years ( Luo et al., Conference Proceedings ; Yu and Long, 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) . These algorithms mainly follow the branch-and-bound framework by deciding which vertices should be included in the target k k -biplex, and they reduce the number of branches with carefully-designed branching and pruning strategies. However, these algorithms are mainly effective for small k k values, and their performance substantially degrades when k k becomes large, as shown in Table 3 . For example, on most real-world graphs, existing algorithms struggle to solve most test cases when k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 . In particular, on the dataset Aol , existing algorithms fail to handle any test cases even when k ≥ 2 k\geq 2 . Notably, several studies have proposed algorithms for maximal k k -biplex enumeration ( Yu et al., 2021 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2022 ; Dai et al., 2024 ) . A natural way to apply these algorithms to the maximum k k -biplex search problem is to enumerate all maximal k k -biplexes and then select the one with the maximum number of edges. However, the number of maximal k k -biplexes in a bipartite graph can be exponential with respect to the graph size. Directly applying these enumeration algorithms may generate a large number of maximal but non-maximum k k -biplexes, thereby causing a large amount of unnecessary computation and making them inefficient in practice. Consequently, developing a theoretically and practically efficient algorithm for the maximum k k -biplex search remains a challenging task. Contributions. To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose a novel deletion-based algorithm for the maximum k k -biplex search problem with a non-trivial worst-case time complexity. We also propose several optimization techniques to further improve the practical performance of the algorithm. The main contributions of this paper are as follows. A novel deletion-based algorithm. We reveal the structural connection between maximum k k -biplex search in the original bipartite graph and k k -bounded-degree deletion in the complement graph. Based on this connection, we propose a deletion-based algorithm for maximum k k -biplex search. Specifically, we first propose a novel deletion-based branching strategy, which decides which vertices to be deleted from the subgraph. We then develop several branch reduction techniques to further enhance the performance of the deletion-based branching strategy. Finally, we prove that our deletion-based algorithm achieves a non-trivial worst-case time complexity of O ∗ ​ ( γ k n ) O^{*}(\gamma_{k}^{n}) . When k = 1 , 2 k=1,2 and 3 3 , we have γ 1 = 1.725 \gamma_{1}=1.725 , γ 2 = 1.856 \gamma_{2}=1.856 and γ 3 = 1.928 \gamma_{3}=1.928 , respectively. To the best of our knowledge, our algorithm achieves the best known time complexity among all existing algorithms for maximum k k -biplex search. Efficient optimization techniques. To further improve the practical performance of the proposed deletion-based algorithm, we design several optimization techniques tailored to the deletion-based search framework. Specifically, we propose two efficient edge upper bounds to prune search branches that cannot generate a larger k k -biplex. The first upper bound is derived from the newly added vertex and limits how many of its non-neighbors can still be kept; the second upper bound is derived from the total missing-edge allowance of the current partial solution on one side. We show that these upper bounds can be computed in linear time for each search instance. Finally, we develop a heuristic algorithm to quickly construct a large initial k k -biplex in polynomial time, combining a greedy deletion stage with a localized expansion stage based on the distance property of large k k -biplexes. Comprehensive experiments. We conduct extensive experiments on 8 real-world bipartite graphs to evaluate the efficiency and scalability of our proposed algorithm. We compare our algorithm with two state-of-the-art maximum k k -biplex search algorithms under various settings of k k and θ \theta . The experimental results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm substantially outperforms existing solutions, achieving up to four orders of magnitude speedups. For example, our algorithm solves all test cases on the graph Aol , while the baseline algorithms fail to solve most test cases within 24 hours. More specifically, our algorithm finds a maximum 4 4 -biplex on Aol with both side sizes larger than 17 17 in only 6.14 6.14 seconds, while the other two baseline algorithms cannot finish within 24 hours, demonstrating that our algorithm is up to four orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art approaches.

sections.heading: 2.1. Existing Solutions
sections.text: Several exact approaches have been proposed to solve the maximum k k -biplex search problem ( Yu and Long, 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) . Below, we briefly review their main technical ideas and limitations. Yu et al. ( Yu and Long, 2023 ) studied the problem of finding K K maximal k k -biplexes with the most edges, where K = 1 K=1 corresponds to our problem. They proposed a branch-and-bound algorithm based on a symmetric Bron–Kerbosch branching strategy. Specifically, the algorithm chooses a pivot vertex u u with at least k + 1 k+1 non-neighbors v 1 , v 2 , … , v k + 1 v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{k+1} in the current subgraph, and then generates subbranches in the following way: the first branch excludes u u from the subgraph, and the i + 1 i+1 -th branch excludes v i v_{i} while adding u , v 1 , … , v i − 1 u,v_{1},\ldots,v_{i-1} into the k k -biplex. Since u u has at most k k non-neighbors in a k k -biplex, at most k + 2 k+2 subbranches will be generated. With this branching strategy, their algorithm achieves a worst-case time complexity O ∗ ​ ( α k n ) O^{*}(\alpha_{k}^{n}) , where α k < 2 \alpha_{k}<2 ; when k = 1 , 2 , k=1,2, and 3 3 , α k = 1.754 , 1.888 , \alpha_{k}=1.754,1.888, and 1.947 1.947 , respectively. This branching strategy is effective when k k is small, but becomes less efficient when k k increases. This is because the number of subbranches generated by the symmetric-BK branching strategy depends heavily on k k . When k k increases, the rapid increase in the number of branches results in an excessively large search space, thereby reducing search efficiency. Pan et al. ( Pan et al., 2024 ) studied the maximum k k -biplex search problem over large bipartite graphs and proposed a core-based graph reduction framework. Specifically, for every possible side-size pair ( x , y ) (x,y) of the target k k -biplex, they compute the corresponding ( x , y ) (x,y) -core, where vertices on the two sides have degree at least y − k y-k and x − k x-k , respectively. The algorithm then examines every pair ( x , y ) (x,y) in decreasing order of the value x ⋅ y x\cdot y . For the current pair ( x , y ) (x,y) , it runs branch-and-bound search on the corresponding ( x , y ) (x,y) -core to find a k k -biplex S = ( U S , V S , E S ) S=(U_{S},V_{S},E_{S}) with | U S | = x |U_{S}|=x and | V S | = y |V_{S}|=y . Once such a solution is found, all remaining pairs ( x ′ , y ′ ) (x^{\prime},y^{\prime}) with x ′ ⋅ y ′ ≤ | E S | x^{\prime}\cdot y^{\prime}\leq|E_{S}| can be safely discarded, because no k k -biplex with these side sizes can contain more than x ′ ⋅ y ′ x^{\prime}\cdot y^{\prime} edges. If no such k k -biplex is found in the current core, the algorithm continues to the next pair. However, the effectiveness of this core-based reduction decreases as k k becomes large. For a fixed side-size pair ( x , y ) (x,y) , the degree requirements of the corresponding core are y − k y-k and x − k x-k , respectively. Thus, a larger k k directly lowers these requirements and allows more vertices to remain in the reduced graph. As a result, the branch-and-bound search is still conducted on a large core. Moreover, since a larger k k allows more missing edges in the target k k -biplex, the pruning rules become less restrictive, further increasing the search cost.

sections.heading: 3. A Novel Deletion-based Algorithm
sections.text: In this section, we propose a novel deletion-based algorithm for the maximum k k -biplex search problem, which solves the problem from the complement graph: instead of deciding which vertices should be kept in the original graph, we decide which vertices should be deleted so that the remaining complement subgraph has bounded degree. We prove that our algorithm achieves a non-trivial worst-case time complexity of O ∗ ​ ( γ k n ) O^{*}(\gamma_{k}^{n}) , where γ k < 2 \gamma_{k}<2 . For example, when k = 1 , 2 k=1,2 and 3 3 , we have γ 1 = 1.725 \gamma_{1}=1.725 , γ 2 = 1.856 \gamma_{2}=1.856 and γ 3 = 1.928 \gamma_{3}=1.928 , respectively. To the best of our knowledge, our algorithm achieves the best known time complexity among all existing algorithms for maximum k k -biplex search.

sections.heading: 3.1. Deletion-based Branching Framework
sections.text: We first introduce the concept of deletion in bipartite graphs. Given a bipartite graph G = ( U , V , E ) G=(U,V,E) , the k k -bounded-degree deletion of G G is defined as follows. Definition 1 ( k k -bounded-degree deletion). Given a bipartite graph G = ( U , V , E ) G=(U,V,E) and a positive integer k k , a k k -bounded-degree deletion of G G is a vertex subset D ⊆ U ∪ V D\subseteq U\cup V such that after deleting all vertices in D D from G G , the maximum degree of the remaining subgraph G ⁡ [ ( U ∪ V ) ∖ D ] G[(U\cup V)\setminus D] is at most k k . For convenience of discussion, we refer to a k k -bounded-degree deletion as a k k -BDD in this paper. We say a k k -BDD D D is minimal in G G if there is no other k k -BDD D ′ D^{\prime} in G G satisfying that D ′ ⊂ D D^{\prime}\subset D . We then discuss the relationship between k k -biplex and k k -BDD in bipartite graphs. Given a k k -biplex S S of G G , let D = ( U ∪ V ) ∖ S D=(U\cup V)\setminus S . Since every vertex in S S has at most k k non-neighbors in G ⁡ [ S ] G[S] , the maximum degree of G ¯ ​ [ S ] \overline{G}[S] is at most k k . Hence, D D is a k k -BDD of G ¯ \overline{G} . Conversely, if D D is a k k -BDD of G ¯ \overline{G} , then the remaining vertex set ( U ∪ V ) ∖ D (U\cup V)\setminus D induces a k k -biplex in G G . However, this correspondence does not mean that the maximum k k -biplex can be obtained by finding a k k -BDD that leaves the fewest edges in the complement graph. For example, consider k = 1 k=1 and θ = 2 \theta=2 . Let U = { u 1 , u 2 , u 3 } U=\{u_{1},u_{2},u_{3}\} and V = { v 1 , v 2 , v 3 } V=\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\} , and let G G contain all edges except ( u 3 , v 3 ) (u_{3},v_{3}) . Then G ⁡ [ U ∪ V ] G[U\cup V] is a 1 1 -biplex with eight edges, and thus it is the maximum 1 1 -biplex. In G ¯ \overline{G} , this solution leaves one complement edge. In contrast, if we keep only { u 1 , u 2 } ∪ { v 1 , v 2 } \{u_{1},u_{2}\}\cup\{v_{1},v_{2}\} , the remaining complement graph has no edge, but the corresponding subgraph of G G has only four edges, and hence is not the maximum k k -biplex of G G . To overcome this limitation, we develop the new relationship between the maximum k k -biplex of G G and the k k -BDD of G ¯ \overline{G} , which builds upon the following lemma. Lemma 0 . Given a bipartite graph G = ( U , V , E ) G=(U,V,E) and a maximum k k -biplex G ⁡ [ S ] = ( U S , V S , E S ) G[S]=(U_{S},V_{S},E_{S}) of G G , ( U ∪ V ) ∖ S (U\cup V)\setminus S forms a minimal k k -BDD of G ¯ \overline{G} . Proof. We prove this lemma by contradiction. Let D = ( U ∪ V ) ∖ S D=(U\cup V)\setminus S . If there exists a minimal k k -BDD D ′ D^{\prime} in G ¯ \overline{G} satisfying D ′ ⊂ D D^{\prime}\subset D , we have S = ( U ∪ V ) ∖ D ⊂ ( U ∪ V ) ∖ D ′ S=(U\cup V)\setminus D\subset(U\cup V)\setminus D^{\prime} , which means G ⁡ [ ( U ∪ V ) ∖ D ′ ] G[(U\cup V)\setminus D^{\prime}] forms a k k -biplex that contains G ⁡ [ S ] G[S] , contradicting the maximality. Therefore, G ⁡ [ S ] G[S] is not a maximum k k -biplex of G G , which contradicts the condition. ∎ Based on this lemma, we propose a new structural duality that a maximum k k -biplex of G G always corresponds to a specific minimal k k -BDD of G ¯ \overline{G} , as shown in the following theorem. Theorem 3 (Structural Duality) . Let G = ( U , V , E ) G=(U,V,E) be a bipartite graph and G ¯ = ( U , V , E ¯ ) \overline{G}=(U,V,\overline{E}) be its complement. If a minimal k k -BDD D = ( U D , V D ) D=(U_{D},V_{D}) of G ¯ \overline{G} satisfies | U D | ≤ | U | − θ \lvert U_{D}\rvert\leq\lvert U\rvert-\theta and | V D | ≤ | V | − θ \lvert V_{D}\rvert\leq\lvert V\rvert-\theta , and maximizes | U ∖ U D | × | V ∖ V D | − | E ¯ ( U ∪ V ) ∖ D | \lvert U\setminus U_{D}\rvert\times\lvert V\setminus V_{D}\rvert-\lvert\overline{E}_{(U\cup V)\setminus D}\rvert among all minimal k k -BDDs in G ¯ \overline{G} satisfying these two constraints, then G ⁡ [ U ∪ V ∖ D ] G[U\cup V\setminus D] is a maximum k k -biplex of G G . Proof. Let S = ( U ∖ U D , V ∖ V D ) S=(U\setminus U_{D},V\setminus V_{D}) . Since D D is a k k -BDD of G ¯ \overline{G} , the maximum degree of G ¯ ​ [ S ] \overline{G}[S] is at most k k . Equivalently, every vertex in G ⁡ [ S ] G[S] has at most k k non-neighbors. Thus, G ⁡ [ S ] G[S] is a k k -biplex. As | U D | ≤ | U | − θ \lvert U_{D}\rvert\leq\lvert U\rvert-\theta and | V D | ≤ | V | − θ \lvert V_{D}\rvert\leq\lvert V\rvert-\theta , we have | U S | = | U ∖ U D | ≥ θ \lvert U_{S}\rvert=\lvert U\setminus U_{D}\rvert\geq\theta and | V S | = | V ∖ V D | ≥ θ \lvert V_{S}\rvert=\lvert V\setminus V_{D}\rvert\geq\theta . Since | E S | = | U S | × | V S | − | E ¯ S | = | U ∖ U D | × | V ∖ V D | − | E ¯ ( U ∪ V ) ∖ D | |E_{S}|=|U_{S}|\times|V_{S}|-|\overline{E}_{S}|=\lvert U\setminus U_{D}\rvert\times\lvert V\setminus V_{D}\rvert-\lvert\overline{E}_{(U\cup V)\setminus D}\rvert , and the complement vertex set of a maximum k k -biplex of G G is always a minimal k k -BDD of G ¯ \overline{G} according to Lemma 2 , maximizing | E S | |E_{S}| among all k k -biplexes in G G is equivalent to maximizing | U ∖ U D | × | V ∖ V D | − | E ¯ ( U ∪ V ) ∖ D | \lvert U\setminus U_{D}\rvert\times\lvert V\setminus V_{D}\rvert-\lvert\overline{E}_{(U\cup V)\setminus D}\rvert among all minimal k k -BDDs in G ¯ \overline{G} . ∎ Theorem 3 reformulates the maximum k k -biplex search problem as finding a specific minimal k k -BDD in the complement graph. Based on this formulation, we develop deletion-based branching and reduction strategies tailored to the maximum k k -biplex search problem. Specifically, given a bipartite graph G = ( U , V , E ) G=(U,V,E) and its complement graph G ¯ = ( U , V , E ¯ ) \overline{G}=(U,V,\overline{E}) , let ( D , S , C ) (D,S,C) be an instance of our deletion-based algorithm, where D ⊆ U ∪ V D\subseteq U\cup V is the partial deletion set containing vertices that have been deleted from G ¯ \overline{G} , S ⊆ U ∪ V S\subseteq U\cup V is the partial k k -biplex set containing vertices that cannot be deleted from G ¯ \overline{G} (i.e., the vertices that must be kept in the maximum k k -biplex), and C ⊆ U ∪ V C\subseteq U\cup V is the candidate set containing vertices to be moved to D D or S S . The three sets are disjoint, and G ⁡ [ S ] G[S] is maintained as a valid k k -biplex throughout the search. The instance ( D , S , C ) (D,S,C) aims to find a minimal k k -BDD D ∗ ⊆ C D^{*}\subseteq C in G ¯ ​ [ S ∪ C ] \overline{G}[S\cup C] such that G ⁡ [ ( U ∪ V ) ∖ ( D ∪ D ∗ ) ] G[(U\cup V)\setminus(D\cup D^{*})] is a maximum k k -biplex of G ⁡ [ S ∪ C ] G[S\cup C] containing S S . In particular, the initial instance ( ( ∅ , ∅ ) , ( ∅ , ∅ ) , ( U , V ) ) ((\emptyset,\emptyset),(\emptyset,\emptyset),(U,V)) aims to find such a k k -BDD in G ¯ \overline{G} , which corresponds to a maximum k k -biplex of G G . Given an instance ( D , S , C ) (D,S,C) , our algorithm selects a vertex u ∈ S ∪ C u\in S\cup C and generate subbranches in the following way: if the selected vertex is in C C , generate one subbranch that moves it to D D ; the remaining branches handle the cases where it is kept in S S . For convenience, we refer to such a vertex u u as a branching vertex of the current instance ( D , S , C ) (D,S,C) . Our algorithm then recursively applies this branching method until D D forms a minimal k k -BDD of G ¯ \overline{G} , where G ⁡ [ S ∪ C ] G[S\cup C] gives a candidate solution for the maximum k k -biplex of G G . More specifically, our deletion-based branching strategy relies on the following branching rule. Theorem 4 (Deletion-based branching rule) . Given a bipartite graph G G and a vertex v v of G G , any k k -BDD of G ¯ \overline{G} must contain either v v or at least d ¯ ​ ( v ) − k \overline{d}(v)-k of v v ’s neighbors in G ¯ \overline{G} . Proof. Consider a k k -BDD D D of G ¯ \overline{G} . If v ∈ D v\in D , the theorem holds directly. Otherwise, v v remains in G ¯ ∖ D \overline{G}\setminus D . According to the definition of k k -BDD, at most k k neighbors of v v in G ¯ \overline{G} can remain together with v v . Therefore, at least d ¯ ​ ( v ) − k \overline{d}(v)-k neighbors of v v in G ¯ \overline{G} must be contained in D D . ∎ According to Theorem 4 , selecting a branching vertex u ∈ C u\in C with a large degree in G ¯ ​ [ S ∪ C ] \overline{G}[S\cup C] creates a strong branching condition: once u u is kept, at least d ¯ S ∪ C ​ ( u ) − k \overline{d}_{S\cup C}(u)-k vertices in N ¯ C ​ ( u ) \overline{N}_{C}(u) must be deleted. Therefore, to delete as many vertices as possible from C C , we can choose u ∈ C u\in C with the maximum value of d ¯ S ∪ C ​ ( u ) \overline{d}_{S\cup C}(u) . The new subinstances are generated as follows. (1) If r ≤ 0 r\leq 0 , D D forms a minimal k k -BDD of G ¯ \overline{G} , update the current best solution with G ⁡ [ S ∪ C ] G[S\cup C] and return. (2) If u ∈ C u\in C , generate one subinstance ( D ∪ { u } , S , C ∖ { u } ) (D\cup\{u\},S,C\setminus\{u\}) , corresponding to the case where u u is deleted. After this subinstance returns, add u u to S S . sections.text: We introduce several branch reductions to further enhance the efficiency of our deletion-based branching strategy. First, we reduce C C through vertices with a large number of non-neighbors in S S . Lemma 0 (Branch Reduction 1) . Given an instance ( D , S , C ) (D,S,C) and a vertex u ∈ C u\in C , if d ¯ S ​ ( u ) > k \overline{d}_{S}(u)>k or there exists v ∈ N ¯ S ​ ( u ) v\in\overline{N}_{S}(u) satisfying d ¯ S ​ ( v ) ≥ k \overline{d}_{S}(v)\geq k , we can move u u from C C to D D directly. Proof. We prove it by contradiction. If d ¯ S ​ ( u ) > k \overline{d}_{S}(u)>k and u u is not included in any k k -BDD D ′ D^{\prime} derived from ( D , S , C ) (D,S,C) , then u u will have more than k k neighbors in G ¯ ​ [ ( S ∪ C ) ∖ D ′ ] \overline{G}[(S\cup C)\setminus D^{\prime}] and thus D ′ D^{\prime} is not a k k -BDD of G ¯ \overline{G} . Similarly, if there exists v ∈ N ¯ S ​ ( u ) v\in\overline{N}_{S}(u) with d ¯ S ​ ( v ) ≥ k \overline{d}_{S}(v)\geq k , then v v will have at least k + 1 k+1 neighbors in G ¯ ​ [ ( S ∪ C ) ∖ D ′ ] \overline{G}[(S\cup C)\setminus D^{\prime}] and thereby D ′ D^{\prime} is not a k k -BDD of G ¯ \overline{G} as well. ∎ Then, we reduce C C through vertices that cannot be contained in any k k -biplex satisfying the size threshold θ \theta . Lemma 0 (Branch Reduction 2) . Given an instance ( D , S , C ) (D,S,C) and a vertex u ∈ C u\in C , if d S ∪ C ​ ( u ) < θ − k d_{S\cup C}(u)<\theta-k , we can move u u from C C to D D directly. Proof. Assume that a k k -biplex S ′ S^{\prime} derived from ( D , S , C ) (D,S,C) contains u u . Since the opposite side of u u in S ′ S^{\prime} has at least θ \theta vertices, vertex u u must have at least θ − k \theta-k neighbors in S ′ S^{\prime} . However, S ′ ⊆ S ∪ C S^{\prime}\subseteq S\cup C , and hence d S ′ ​ ( u ) ≤ d S ∪ C ​ ( u ) < θ − k d_{S^{\prime}}(u)\leq d_{S\cup C}(u)<\theta-k , a contradiction. Therefore, u u cannot be contained in any solution and can be moved to D D . ∎ Intuitively, if adding a candidate vertex from C C to S S does not make itself or any of its non-neighbors violate the k k -biplex constraint, then keeping this vertex can only enlarge the solution. This leads to the following reduction. Lemma 0 (Branch Reduction 3) . Given an instance ( D , S , C ) (D,S,C) and a vertex u ∈ C u\in C , if ∀ v ∈ { u } ∪ N ¯ S ∪ C ​ ( u ) , d ¯ S ∪ C ​ ( v ) ≤ k \forall v\in\{u\}\cup\overline{N}_{S\cup C}(u),\overline{d}_{S\cup C}(v)\leq k , we can move u u from C C to S S directly. Proof. Let S ′ S^{\prime} be any k k -biplex derived from ( D , S , C ) (D,S,C) that does not contain u u . We show that S ′ ∪ { u } S^{\prime}\cup\{u\} is still a k k -biplex. Since d ¯ S ∪ C ​ ( u ) ≤ k \overline{d}_{S\cup C}(u)\leq k and S ′ ∪ { u } ⊆ S ∪ C S^{\prime}\cup\{u\}\subseteq S\cup C , vertex u u has at most k k non-neighbors in S ′ ∪ { u } S^{\prime}\cup\{u\} . Furthermore, for any vertex v ∈ N ¯ S ′ ​ ( u ) v\in\overline{N}_{S^{\prime}}(u) , we have d ¯ S ′ ∪ { u } ​ ( v ) ≤ d ¯ S ∪ C ​ ( v ) ≤ k \overline{d}_{S^{\prime}\cup\{u\}}(v)\leq\overline{d}_{S\cup C}(v)\leq k . The non-degrees of all other vertices in S ′ S^{\prime} remain unchanged after adding u u to S ′ S^{\prime} . Thus, after adding u u , S ′ ∪ { u } S^{\prime}\cup\{u\} is still a k k -biplex. ∎ We notice that the branching size can be further reduced for the case δ ¯ S ∪ C = k + 1 \overline{\delta}_{S\cup C}=k+1 . In this case, every vertex in G ¯ ​ [ S ∪ C ] \overline{G}[S\cup C] has at most k + 1 k+1 neighbors. This branch reduction is based on the following lemma. Lemma 0 (Branch reduction 4) . Given an instance ( D , S , C ) (D,S,C) and a vertex u ∈ C u\in C . If d ¯ S ∪ C ​ ( u ) ≤ k \overline{d}_{S\cup C}(u)\leq k , and u u has exactly one neighbor v v in G ¯ ​ [ S ∪ C ] \overline{G}[S\cup C] satisfying d ¯ S ∪ C ​ ( v ) > k \overline{d}_{S\cup C}(v)>k , and v v has exactly k + 1 k+1 neighbors in G ¯ ​ [ S ∪ C ] \overline{G}[S\cup C] , then after moving u u to D D , we can add v v and all vertices in N ¯ C ​ ( v ) ∖ { u } \overline{N}_{C}(v)\setminus\{u\} to S S directly. Proof. We prove it by contradiction. Let D ′ D^{\prime} be a minimal k k -BDD derived from the current instance that contains u u and at least one vertex from { v } ∪ N ¯ C ​ ( v ) ∖ { u } \{v\}\cup\overline{N}_{C}(v)\setminus\{u\} . Let S ′ = S ∪ C ∖ D ′ S^{\prime}=S\cup C\setminus D^{\prime} be the k k -biplex derived from deleting D ′ D^{\prime} . If v ∈ D ′ v\in D^{\prime} , we have d ¯ S ′ ​ ( u ) < k \overline{d}_{S^{\prime}}(u)<k and every neighbor x x of u u in G ¯ ​ [ S ′ ] \overline{G}[S^{\prime}] satisfies d ¯ S ′ ​ ( x ) < k \overline{d}_{S^{\prime}}(x)<k . Therefore, D ′ ∖ { u } D^{\prime}\setminus\{u\} is still a k k -BDD and thus D ′ D^{\prime} is not minimal. If there exists a vertex w ∈ N ¯ C ​ ( v ) ∖ { u } w\in\overline{N}_{C}(v)\setminus\{u\} and w ∈ D ′ w\in D^{\prime} , then we have d ¯ S ′ ​ ( v ) < k \overline{d}_{S^{\prime}}(v)<k , and every neighbor x x of u u in G ¯ ​ [ S ′ ] \overline{G}[S^{\prime}] except v v satisfies d ¯ S ′ ​ ( x ) < k \overline{d}_{S^{\prime}}(x)<k . Therefore, D ′ ∖ { u } D^{\prime}\setminus\{u\} is also a k k -BDD and thus D ′ D^{\prime} is not minimal. ∎ Figure 2. sections.heading: 4. Optimization Techniques
sections.text: In this section, we propose several optimization techniques to further enhance the practical performance of our deletion-based algorithm, including efficient upper-bounding techniques to prune unnecessary instances in linear time and a new heuristic algorithm to identify an initial near-maximum k k -biplex in polynomial time.

sections.heading: 5.1. Experimental Setup
sections.text: Datasets. We use 8 real-world bipartite graphs from diverse categories to evaluate the efficiency of our algorithm. These graphs have been widely used as benchmark datasets for bipartite cohesive subgraph search problems ( Lyu et al., 2020 ; Yu and Long, 2023 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) . The detailed information of these graphs is shown in Table 2 , where δ \delta represents the maximum degree of vertices on each side. All these datasets are publicly available at http://konect.cc/networks . Algorithms. We implement our proposed deletion-based algorithm in Algorithm 1 , denoted by DMBP , which is equipped with all optimization techniques described in Sec. 4.1 . We also implement two state-of-the-art maximum k k -biplex search algorithms for comparative analysis, namely FastBB and CMBS-CSS . Specifically, FastBB is a branch-and-bound algorithm that adopts the symmetric-BK branching strategy, which achieves a non-trivial worst-case time complexity ( Yu and Long, 2023 ) . CMBS-CSS is a core-based algorithm that combines the symmetric-BK branching strategy with a core-based pruning method ( Pan et al., 2024 ) . All algorithms are implemented in C++ and executed on a PC equipped with a 2.2GHz CPU and 128GB RAM running Linux . Parameter settings. During the evaluations of all algorithms, we vary k k from 1 1 to 6 6 . Following the size constraint in Sec. 2, we choose θ \theta from the range [ 2 ​ k + 1 , 20 ] [2k+1,20] for each k k . We report the CPU time in seconds, excluding the time for reading graphs from external storage. sections.text: Exp-1: Efficiency comparison among different algorithms. We evaluate the efficiency of DMBP and two baseline algorithms, FastBB and CMBS-CSS , on 8 real-world graphs. The results are shown in Table 3 , where the column | E ∗ | \lvert E^{*}\rvert represents the number of edges in the maximum k k -biplex, and the notion “-” represents a timeout exceeding 24 hours. A value | E ∗ | = 0 |E^{*}|=0 means that no k k -biplex satisfying the size threshold exists for this parameter setting. As observed, DMBP consistently outperforms the baseline algorithms across most input parameters. Specifically, DMBP solves all 96 test cases, while FastBB and CMBS-CSS solve only 23 and 22 test cases, respectively. The advantage becomes more evident when k k is large: among the 64 test cases with k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 , FastBB and CMBS-CSS solve only 4 and 2 test cases, respectively. For example, on LKML with k = 2 k=2 and θ = 9 \theta=9 , DMBP completes in 2.77 2.77 s, while FastBB and CMBS-CSS take 16,231 16,231 s and 15,665 15,665 s, respectively, achieving at least 5000 × 5000\times speedups. On Mummun with k = 4 k=4 and θ = 19 \theta=19 , DMBP completes in 0.33 0.33 s, while CMBS-CSS takes 9,257 9,257 s and FastBB times out, achieving at least 28000 × 28000\times speedups. Notably, DMBP solves all test cases on Aol with varying k k from 1 1 to 6 6 . In contrast, the two baseline algorithms fail to solve any test cases on this graph when k ≥ 2 k\geq 2 , and CMBS-CSS barely managed to finish when k = 1 k=1 and θ = 8 \theta=8 in 21 hours. These results demonstrate the high efficiency of our proposed algorithm, especially with large k k values. Exp-2: Efficiency with varying θ \theta and k k . We evaluate the performance of DMBP and the two baseline algorithms FastBB and CMBS-CSS by varying θ \theta and k k on two representative datasets, IMDB and Google . Similar results can be obtained on other datasets. The results are shown in Fig. 4 , where the notion “INF” represents a timeout. As observed, DMBP consistently outperforms the baselines under different parameter settings, achieving speedups up to 100 × 100\times . For example, on the graph IMDB with k = 4 k=4 and θ = 16 \theta=16 shown in Fig. 4 (c), our algorithm takes only 80 80 seconds, while CMBS-CSS takes over 1000 1000 seconds and FastBB cannot finish in 24 hours. However, the runtime curve of DMBP grows much more slowly than those of the baselines, while FastBB and CMBS-CSS frequently reach the timeout on hard k k or θ \theta settings. The results are shown in Fig. 5 . As observed, incorporating the upper-bounding techniques significantly improves the efficiency of DMBP . sections.heading: 6. Related Works
sections.text: Maximal k k -biplex enumeration. Closely related to our work is the maximal k k -biplex enumeration problem, which aims to find all k k -biplexes not contained in any larger ones. This problem has attracted increasing attention in recent years ( Yu et al., 2022 ; Yu et al., 2021 ; Dai et al., 2024 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Sim et al., 2009 ) . Sim et al. ( Sim et al., 2009 ) first defined the k k -biplex as a type of quasi-biclique and proposed a basic branch-and-bound algorithm MQBminer to enumerate all maximal k k -biplexes satisfying a vertex size constraint. Although it uses degree-based and common-neighbor-based pruning methods, MQBminer still generates many redundant branches. To address this, Yu et al. ( Yu et al., 2021 ) proposed iMB , a prefix-based algorithm equipped with early stopping strategies to reduce redundant non-maximal branches. However, its performance degrades on graphs with millions of edges when k > 2 k>2 . Yu et al. ( Yu et al., 2021 ) also introduced iTraversal , a polynomial-delay algorithm based on a reverse search framework. While it guarantees polynomial time between outputs, it requires storing all maximal k k -biplexes in memory, making it unsuitable for large-scale graphs. Alternatively, Dai et al. ( Dai et al., 2023 ) proposed a pivot-based algorithm that uses pivoting techniques to avoid numerous non-maximal branches. However, it still suffers from a trivial worst-case time complexity of O ∗ ​ ( 2 n ) O^{*}(2^{n}) . To overcome this, Dai et al. ( Dai et al., 2024 ) later developed two algorithms combining pivoting techniques with a binary branching strategy. These two algorithms achieve non-trivial time complexities and currently offer the best practical performance when k ≤ 6 k\leq 6 . These algorithms can be adapted to maximum k k -biplex search by enumerating all maximal k k -biplexes and returning the one with the most edges. However, since the number of maximal k k -biplexes can be exponential in the graph size, this approach may enumerate many maximal but non-maximum k k -biplexes, causing substantial unnecessary computation in practice. Maximum k k -plex search. The maximum k k -plex search problem aims to find a k k -plex with the most vertices in traditional graphs, where the k k -plex model was originally introduced in ( Seidman and Foster, 1978 ) . This domain encompasses various formulations, among which the maximum k k -plex search problem is the closest to our work and has been proven to be NP-hard ( Lewis and Yannakakis, 1980 ) . Many approaches have been proposed to address this challenge. On the one hand, some approaches focus on carefully designed branching rules to surpass the trivial O ∗ ​ ( 2 n ) O^{*}(2^{n}) barrier, including strategies that prioritize vertices based on non-neighbor counts to strictly limit worst-case complexity ( Chang and Yao, 2024 ; Xiao et al., Conference Proceedings ) . Notably, Wang et al. ( Wang et al., 2023 ) developed a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm by exploiting the dual problem of the maximum k k -plex search and derived a worst-case time complexity of O ∗ ​ ( ( k + 1 ) g ) O^{*}((k+1)^{g}) , where g g represents the gap between the degeneracy and the size of maximum k k -plex. On the other hand, some approaches target scalability on large-scale graphs by using graph reductions based on degree and common-neighbor constraints ( Chang et al., 2022 ; Gao et al., Conference Proceedings ; Zhou et al., Conference Proceedings ) , as well as new upper bounds derived from vertex coloring and vertex partitioning ( Zhou et al., Conference Proceedings ; Jiang et al., 2021 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., Conference Proceedings ) , to prune unnecessary branches. Notably, Ahmad et al. ( Ahmad et al., 2025 ) synthesized these state-of-the-art techniques into a comprehensive framework to identify optimal configurations for general scenarios. However, these approaches are designed to maximize the number of vertices in traditional graphs, which is quite different from our problem of maximizing the number of edges in bipartite graphs, so these methods cannot be directly applied to the maximum k k -biplex search problem.

sections.heading: 7. Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we investigate the maximum k k -biplex search problem in bipartite graphs. We propose a novel deletion-based algorithm that reformulates the problem as finding a minimal k k -bounded degree deletion in the complement graph. Based on this formulation, DMBP employs a new deletion-based branching strategy and branch reduction rules, achieving a worst-case time complexity below O ∗ ​ ( 2 n ) O^{*}(2^{n}) . In addition, we develop several optimization techniques to further improve practical efficiency, including effective upper bounds and a heuristic algorithm. Extensive experiments on 8 real-world bipartite graphs demonstrate the efficiency and scalability of our deletion-based algorithm and the proposed optimization techniques.

Biplex, as a relaxation of the biclique model, has emerged as an important cohesive subgraph model for bipartite graph analysis. The maximum k k -biplex search problem aims to identify the k k -biplex with maximum number of edges and has been widely applied in various real-world applications, including community detection, online recommendation, and fraud detection. However, the problem is NP-hard, and existing exact algorithms remain inefficient on large-scale bipartite graphs with large values of k k (e.g., k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 ). In this paper, we revisit the maximum k k -biplex search problem from a complementary perspective. We reveal a novel structural duality: finding a maximum k k -biplex in a bipartite graph is equivalent to finding a minimal k k -bounded-degree deletion in its complement graph. Based on this observation, we propose a novel deletion-based algorithm for the maximum k k -biplex search problem. We theoretically prove that the proposed algorithm achieves a worst-case time complexity of O ∗ ​ ( γ k n ) O^{*}(\gamma_{k}^{n}) , where γ k < 2 \gamma_{k}<2 . Specifically, γ 1 = 1.725 \gamma_{1}=1.725 , γ 2 = 1.856 \gamma_{2}=1.856 , and γ 3 = 1.928 \gamma_{3}=1.928 . To further enhance practical efficiency, we develop several effective upper-bounding techniques and a heuristic strategy for obtaining high-quality initial solutions, which substantially reduce the search space. Extensive experiments on eight real-world bipartite graphs demonstrate the efficiency of our approach, which achieves up to four orders of magnitude speedups over state-of-the-art algorithms. 1. Introduction Bipartite graphs are fundamental data structures for modeling interactions between two distinct groups of entities, such as user-item interactions in e-commerce networks ( Li et al., 2023 ; Yu and Long, 2023 ) , author-publication relationships in academic networks ( Ley, 2002 ) , and gene-protein associations in computational biology networks ( Voggenreiter et al., 2012 ; Eren et al., 2013 ; Xie et al., 2019 ) . Identifying cohesive subgraphs is a core task in bipartite graph mining, since such subgraphs often reveal meaningful groups with strong cross-side associations. For example, in computational biology networks, cohesive subgraphs can capture groups of genes and proteins with strong expression associations, thereby helping identify functional modules or disease-related biological pathways ( Xie et al., 2019 ) . As a classical cohesive subgraph model in bipartite graphs, the biclique has been widely studied and applied in many scenarios ( Braun et al., 2017 ; Lehmann et al., 2008 ; Langston et al., 2008 ) . A biclique is a complete bipartite subgraph, where every vertex on one side is connected to all vertices on the other side. The maximum biclique search problem aims to find a biclique containing the maximum number of edges, which has attracted considerable attention in recent years ( Liu et al., 2006 ; Alzahrani and Horadam, 2019 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Gillis and Glineur, 2014 ; Feng et al., 2018 ; Lyu et al., 2020 ) . However, real-world network data are inevitably affected by observation noise, measurement errors, and missing data ( Li et al., 2008 ; Liu et al., Conference Proceedings ) . Due to the strict complete-connectivity requirement, the biclique is unable to represent cohesive communities that contain a small number of missing edges, which limits its practical application. To address this limitation, the k k -biplex model was introduced as a relaxation of the biclique and has attracted increasing attention in recent years ( Yu et al., 2022 ; Dai et al., 2024 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2021 ; Luo et al., Conference Proceedings ; Yu and Long, 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) . Formally, in a k k -biplex of a bipartite graph, each vertex has at most k k non-neighbors. This relaxation allows limited missing edges while preserving its cohesion, and has been applied to many real-world tasks such as online recommendation ( Gunnemann et al., 2011 ; Poernomo and Gopalkrishnan, 2009 ) , community detection ( Dai et al., 2023 ; Hao et al., 2020 ) , and fraud detection ( Dai et al., 2023 ; Yu and Long, 2023 ) . In this paper, we study the problem of finding a k k -biplex with the maximum number of edges, which is referred to as the maximum k k -biplex search problem. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for any positive integer k k ( Pan et al., 2024 ) , implying that no polynomial-time algorithm exists unless P = NP \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP} . To solve the maximum k k -biplex search problem, several exact algorithms have been developed in recent years ( Luo et al., Conference Proceedings ; Yu and Long, 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) . These algorithms mainly follow the branch-and-bound framework by deciding which vertices should be included in the target k k -biplex, and they reduce the number of branches with carefully-designed branching and pruning strategies. However, these algorithms are mainly effective for small k k values, and their performance substantially degrades when k k becomes large, as shown in Table 3 . For example, on most real-world graphs, existing algorithms struggle to solve most test cases when k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 . In particular, on the dataset Aol , existing algorithms fail to handle any test cases even when k ≥ 2 k\geq 2 . Notably, several studies have proposed algorithms for maximal k k -biplex enumeration ( Yu et al., 2021 ; Dai et al., 2023 ; Yu et al., 2022 ; Dai et al., 2024 ) . A natural way to apply these algorithms to the maximum k k -biplex search problem is to enumerate all maximal k k -biplexes and then select the one with the maximum number of edges. However, the number of maximal k k -biplexes in a bipartite graph can be exponential with respect to the graph size. Directly applying these enumeration algorithms may generate a large number of maximal but non-maximum k k -biplexes, thereby causing a large amount of unnecessary computation and making them inefficient in practice. Consequently, developing a theoretically and practically efficient algorithm for the maximum k k -biplex search remains a challenging task. Contributions. To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose a novel deletion-based algorithm for the maximum k k -biplex search problem with a non-trivial worst-case time complexity. We also propose several optimization techniques to further improve the practical performance of the algorithm. The main contributions of this paper are as follows. A novel deletion-based algorithm. We reveal the structural connection between maximum k k -biplex search in the original bipartite graph and k k -bounded-degree deletion in the complement graph. Based on this connection, we propose a deletion-based algorithm for maximum k k -biplex search. Specifically, we first propose a novel deletion-based branching strategy, which decides which vertices to be deleted from the subgraph. We then develop several branch reduction techniques to further enhance the performance of the deletion-based branching strategy. Finally, we prove that our deletion-based algorithm achieves a non-trivial worst-case time complexity of O ∗ ​ ( γ k n ) O^{*}(\gamma_{k}^{n}) . When k = 1 , 2 k=1,2 and 3 3 , we have γ 1 = 1.725 \gamma_{1}=1.725 , γ 2 = 1.856 \gamma_{2}=1.856 and γ 3 = 1.928 \gamma_{3}=1.928 , respectively. To the best of our knowledge, our algorithm achieves the best known time complexity among all existing algorithms for maximum k k -biplex search. Efficient optimization techniques. To further improve the practical performance of the proposed deletion-based algorithm, we design several optimization techniques tailored to the deletion-based search framework. Specifically, we propose two efficient edge upper bounds to prune search branches that cannot generate a larger k k -biplex. The first upper bound is derived from the newly added vertex and limits how many of its non-neighbors can still be kept; the second upper bound is derived from the total missing-edge allowance of the current partial solution on one side. We show that these upper bounds can be computed in linear time for each search instance. Finally, we develop a heuristic algorithm to quickly construct a large initial k k -biplex in polynomial time, combining a greedy deletion stage with a localized expansion stage based on the distance property of large k k -biplexes. Comprehensive experiments. We conduct extensive experiments on 8 real-world bipartite graphs to evaluate the efficiency and scalability of our proposed algorithm. We compare our algorithm with two state-of-the-art maximum k k -biplex search algorithms under various settings of k k and θ \theta . The experimental results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm substantially outperforms existing solutions, achieving up to four orders of magnitude speedups. For example, our algorithm solves all test cases on the graph Aol , while the baseline algorithms fail to solve most test cases within 24 hours. More specifically, our algorithm finds a maximum 4 4 -biplex on Aol with both side sizes larger than 17 17 in only 6.14 6.14 seconds, while the other two baseline algorithms cannot finish within 24 hours, demonstrating that our algorithm is up to four orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art approaches. 2. NP-hardness. As established in ( Yu and Long, 2023 ) , the maximum k k -biplex search problem is NP-hard, which implies there is no polynomial algorithm for solving it unless P = NP \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP} . Consequently, it is essential to develop a maximum k k -biplex search algorithm that is both theoretically and practically efficient. a 2.1. Existing Solutions Several exact approaches have been proposed to solve the maximum k k -biplex search problem ( Yu and Long, 2023 ; Pan et al., 2024 ) . Below, we briefly review their main technical ideas and limitations. Yu et al. ( Yu and Long, 2023 ) studied the problem of finding K K maximal k k -biplexes with the most edges, where K = 1 K=1 corresponds to our problem. They proposed a branch-and-bound algorithm based on a symmetric Bron–Kerbosch branching strategy. Specifically, the algorithm chooses a pivot vertex u u with at least k + 1 k+1 non-neighbors v 1 , v 2 , … , v k + 1 v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{k+1} in the current subgraph, and then generates subbranches in the following way: the first branch excludes u u from the subgraph, and the i + 1 i+1 -th branch excludes v i v_{i} while adding u , v 1 , … , v i − 1 u,v_{1},\ldots,v_{i-1} into the k k -biplex. Since u u has at most k k non-neighbors in a k k -biplex, at most k + 2 k+2 subbranches will be generated. With this branching strategy, their algorithm achieves a worst-case time complexity O ∗ ​ ( α k n ) O^{*}(\alpha_{k}^{n}) , where α k < 2 \alpha_{k}<2 ; when k = 1 , 2 , k=1,2, and 3 3 , α k = 1.754 , 1.888 , \alpha_{k}=1.754,1.888, and 1.947 1.947 , respectively. This branching strategy is effective when k k is small, but becomes less efficient when k k increases. This is because the number of subbranches generated by the symmetric-BK branching strategy depends heavily on k k . When k k increases, the rapid increase in the number of branches results in an excessively large search space, thereby reducing search efficiency. Pan et al. ( Pan et al., 2024 ) studied the maximum k k -biplex search problem over large bipartite graphs and proposed a core-based graph reduction framework. Specifically, for every possible side-size pair ( x , y ) (x,y) of the target k k -biplex, they compute the corresponding ( x , y ) (x,y) -core, where vertices on the two sides have degree at least y − k y-k and x − k x-k , respectively. The algorithm then examines every pair ( x , y ) (x,y) in decreasing order of the value x ⋅ y x\cdot y . For the current pair ( x , y ) (x,y) , it runs branch-and-bound search on the corresponding ( x , y ) (x,y) -core to find a k k -biplex S = ( U S , V S , E S ) S=(U_{S},V_{S},E_{S}) with | U S | = x |U_{S}|=x and | V S | = y |V_{S}|=y . Once such a solution is found, all remaining pairs ( x ′ , y ′ ) (x^{\prime},y^{\prime}) with x ′ ⋅ y ′ ≤ | E S | x^{\prime}\cdot y^{\prime}\leq|E_{S}| can be safely discarded, because no k k -biplex with these side sizes can contain more than x ′ ⋅ y ′ x^{\prime}\cdot y^{\prime} edges. If no such k k -biplex is found in the current core, the algorithm continues to the next pair. However, the effectiveness of this core-based reduction decreases as k k becomes large. For a fixed side-size pair ( x , y ) (x,y) , the degree requirements of the corresponding core are y − k y-k and x − k x-k , respectively. Thus, a larger k k directly lowers these requirements and allows more vertices to remain in the reduced graph. As a result, the branch-and-bound search is still conducted on a large core. Moreover, since a larger k k allows more missing edges in the target k k -biplex, the pruning rules become less restrictive, further increasing the search cost. 3. A Novel Deletion-based Algorithm In this section, we propose a novel deletion-based algorithm for the maximum k k -biplex search problem, which solves the problem from the complement graph: instead of deciding which vertices should be kept in the original graph, we decide which vertices should be deleted so that the remaining complement subgraph has bounded degree. We prove that our algorithm achieves a non-trivial worst-case time complexity of O ∗ ​ ( γ k n ) O^{*}(\gamma_{k}^{n}) , where γ k < 2 \gamma_{k}<2 . For example, when k = 1 , 2 k=1,2 and 3 3 , we have γ 1 = 1.725 \gamma_{1}=1.725 , γ 2 = 1.856 \gamma_{2}=1.856 and γ 3 = 1.928 \gamma_{3}=1.928 , respectively. To the best of our knowledge, our algorithm achieves the best known time complexity among all existing algorithms for maximum k k -biplex search. 3.1. Deletion-based Branching Framework We first introduce the concept of deletion in bipartite graphs. Given a bipartite graph G = ( U , V , E ) G=(U,V,E) , the k k -bounded-degree deletion of G G is defined as follows. Definition 1 ( k k -bounded-degree deletion). Given a bipartite graph G = ( U , V , E ) G=(U,V,E) and a positive integer k k , a k k -bounded-degree deletion of G G is a vertex subset D ⊆ U ∪ V D\subseteq U\cup V such that after deleting all vertices in D D from G G , the maximum degree of the remaining subgraph G ⁡ [ ( U ∪ V ) ∖ D ] G[(U\cup V)\setminus D] is at most k k . For convenience of discussion, we refer to a k k -bounded-degree deletion as a k k -BDD in this paper. We say a k k -BDD D D is minimal in G G if there is no other k k -BDD D ′ D^{\prime} in G G satisfying that D ′ ⊂ D D^{\prime}\subset D . We then discuss the relationship between k k -biplex and k k -BDD in bipartite graphs. Given a k k -biplex S S of G G , let D = ( U ∪ V ) ∖ S D=(U\cup V)\setminus S . Since every vertex in S S has at most k k non-neighbors in G ⁡ [ S ] G[S] , the maximum degree of G ¯ ​ [ S ] \overline{G}[S] is at most k k . Hence, D D is a k k -BDD of G ¯ \overline{G} . Conversely, if D D is a k k -BDD of G ¯ \overline{G} , then the remaining vertex set ( U ∪ V ) ∖ D (U\cup V)\setminus D induces a k k -biplex in G G . However, this correspondence does not mean that the maximum k k -biplex can be obtained by finding a k k -BDD that leaves the fewest edges in the complement graph. For example, consider k = 1 k=1 and θ = 2 \theta=2 . Let U = { u 1 , u 2 , u 3 } U=\{u_{1},u_{2},u_{3}\} and V = { v 1 , v 2 , v 3 } V=\{v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\} , and let G G contain all edges except ( u 3 , v 3 ) (u_{3},v_{3}) . Then G ⁡ [ U ∪ V ] G[U\cup V] is a 1 1 -biplex with eight edges, and thus it is the maximum 1 1 -biplex. In G ¯ \overline{G} , this solution leaves one complement edge.
